title: A neurotoxic cryptic peptide arising from TDP-43-dependent cryptic splicing of PKN1

paper_content.abstract: Dysfunction of transactive response DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) drives neurodegeneration in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Alzheimer’s disease (AD), in part through inducing aberrant RNA splicing. However, whether such mis-splicing yields stable, pathogenic proteins remains unclear. Here, we identify a TDP-43–repressed cryptic exon in Protein kinase N1 (PKN1), designated PKN1-5a1, which is activated in ALS patient brains and introduces a premature termination codon. This aberrant transcript escapes nonsense-mediated decay and is translated into a truncated peptide, PKN1-N207 (PKN207), detectable in AD brains with TDP-43 pathology. In mice, PKN207 impairs cognition, memory, and synaptic plasticity. Our findings demonstrate that TDP-43 loss–induced cryptic splicing can generate stable neurotoxic polypeptides, revealing a peptide-mediated mechanism in TDP-43 proteinopathies.
paper_content.introduction:
Transactive response DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is a conserved RNA-binding protein that plays a key role in maintaining RNA splicing fidelity in the nervous system1. By recognizing UG-rich sequences in pre-mRNA, TDP-43 effectively suppresses aberrant insertion of unannotated cryptic exons, thereby ensuring normal expression of key neuronal genes2,3. Loss of TDP-43 function is widely recognized as a core pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)4, and is also commonly observed in frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and Alzheimer’s disease (AD). In FTD, TDP-43 pathology accounts for approximately 40–50% of cases, characterized by neuronal nuclear inclusions, cytoplasmic deposition, and concomitant gliopathy in the frontal and temporal lobes, and is closely associated with distinct clinical subtypes5,6. In AD, abnormal TDP-43 deposition is detected in about 50–70% of patients (with proportions varying across cohorts)1,4,7,8. Notably, limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy (LATE), a special subtype of AD, is strongly linked to cognitive impairment in the elderly8–10.

In recent years, studies have gradually elucidated how loss of TDP-43 function disrupts neuronal gene expression through cryptic splicing and thereby mediates dysfunction1. For example, in STMN2 (Stathmin 2), TDP-43 loss activates an intronic aberrant event and introduces a premature polyadenylation site, causing transcription to terminate prematurely near exon 2 and preventing the production of functional STMN2 protein11,12; in UNC13A (unc-13 homolog A), TDP-43 loss induces insertion of a cryptic exon carrying a premature termination codon (PTC), triggering nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) and markedly downregulating functional UNC13A protein13,14. These mechanisms directly point to impairments in core processes such as axon growth and synaptic release, and are considered to constitute an important molecular basis of TDP-43 proteinopathies11,12,15,16. In addition, because of their specificity in ALS and early activation, cryptic splicing events are becoming potential biomarkers for disease subtyping and diagnosis17–21.

Notably, TDP-43–dependent cryptic splicing does not end solely in “loss of function”. Some events maintain open reading frame (ORF) continuity or retain key domains, thereby generating de novo proteins that participate in pathological processes. In the reported HDGFL2 (hepatoma-derived growth factor-related protein 2) event, the corresponding product can be detected in brain and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of ALS/FTD patients22; cryptic splicing of MYO18A (myosin XVIIIA) likewise produces an unannotated protein that retains functional domains and is hypothesized to be aggregation-prone23. These findings suggest that certain cryptic splicing events may exacerbate the progression of TDP-43 proteinopathies through gain-of-toxicity pathways.

Protein kinase N1 (PKN1) is a serine/threonine kinase involved in multiple processes, including cytoskeletal dynamics, axonal transport, intracellular signal transduction, and synaptic plasticity24,25. PKN1 can bind to neurofilament light chain (NEFL) and phosphorylate its head domain, thereby regulating neurofilament assembly and axonal structural stability26. Its activity is regulated by Rho-family small GTPase Rac1 and phosphoinositide-dependent protein kinase 1 (PDK1), and undergoes translocation or activation under hyperosmotic/stress conditions27. Under apoptotic stimulation, caspase-3 cleaves PKN1 to form a truncated species that is thought to have kinase activity distinct from the full-length conformation and potential toxic effects28.

In this work, we show that TDP-43 loss induces a cryptic splicing event in the PKN1 gene, designated PKN1-5a1, which inserts a 127-bp exon and introduces PTCs. This aberrant transcript partially escapes NMD and is translated into a stable truncated peptide, PKN1-N207 (PKN207). Using a specifically developed antibody, we detect PKN207 in AD brains with TDP-43 pathology. In vivo studies demonstrate that PKN207 expression impairs cognitive function and synaptic plasticity in mice. Proteomic profiling further reveals distinct alterations in neuronal pathways induced by PKN207. Our findings indicate that TDP-43 dysfunction not only causes loss-of-function effects but can also generate stable, neurotoxic polypeptides, revealing a peptide-level pathological mechanism in TDP-43 proteinopathies.
paper_content.results:
TDP-43 knockdown induces PKN1 cryptic splicing and disrupts its protein expression

TDP-43 plays a pivotal role in maintaining RNA splicing fidelity, primarily by suppressing the aberrant insertion of cryptic exons. Loss of TDP-43 function leads to abnormal cryptic splicing in multiple crucial neuronal genes, resulting in a marked reduction of functional protein expression. Among these, STMN2 and UNC13A represent the most extensively studied targets, and their splicing dysregulation has been established as a key molecular event in neurodegenerative diseases1,11–14,29. Furthermore, other genes including PFKP (phosphofructokinase, Platelet), HDGFL2, and GAP43 (growth associated protein 43) have also been reported to be regulated through this mechanism. Notably, the aberrant splicing of STMN2 and GAP43 has been directly validated to impair axonal regeneration, linking these molecular defects to specific pathological phenotypes1,15,21,22,29. To discover additional TDP-43–regulated cryptic splicing events, we knocked down TDP-43 in neuroblastoma M17 cells and performed RNA-seq to systematically identify potential targets. Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) visualization showed that several known cryptic exon events, such as STMN2, PFKP, and HDGFL2, were all repeatedly detected under TDP-43 knockdown1,11,12,15, verifying the reliability of the sequencing data and the sensitivity of splicing-event detection (Supplementary Fig. 1a).

On this basis, we identified an aberrant splicing region between exons 4 and 5 of the PKN1 gene, in which two distinct splicing forms were detected: one involves insertion of a previously unannotated exon (127 bp), designated PKN1-5a1, with genomic coordinates hg38: chr19:14,450,088–14,450,214; the other is an alternative 3’ splice site (A3SS) of 230 bp with coordinates hg38: chr19:14,450,088–14,450,317, designated PKN1-A3SS (Fig. 1a). Among these, the PKN1-A3SS splicing form was previously reported in TDP-43–knockdown HeLa cells30; here, we characterize the PKN1-5a1 exon, a previously unannotated cryptic exon. We define its precise splice boundaries and sequence features, and elucidate its biological significance. Further analysis showed that the two splice sites of PKN1-5a1 are the canonical splice donor “GU” and acceptor “AG” (Fig. 1a), consistent with classical alternative splicing sequence features31; meanwhile, PKN1-5a1 contains multiple stop codons (Supplementary Fig. 1b). We calculated the PSI (percent-spliced-in) value of this region based on RNA-seq data and found that TDP-43 knockdown primarily activates insertion of the 5a1 exon, whereas the A3SS insertion event is relatively infrequent (Fig. 1b), suggesting that PKN1-5a1 may be the major splicing abnormality driven by TDP-43 loss.

We knocked down TDP-43 in multiple human cell types—including M17, HEK-293T, HeLa, and iNeurons (iPSC-derived cortical neurons)—and analyzed PKN1 splicing patterns. The iPSC-derived cortical neurons were obtained by differentiating human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) and validated by MAP2 and NeuN immunostaining (Supplementary Fig. 1j), indicating successful differentiation into mature neurons. In M17 cells, we performed RT-PCR to detect splicing products in this region and observed that, in addition to the normally spliced product, two aberrant bands appeared after TDP-43 knockdown (Fig. 1c), corresponding to insertion of the PKN1-5a1 and A3SS splicing events (Fig. 1d), respectively, indicating that at least two forms of alternative splicing exist in this region. Subsequent qRT-PCR analysis showed that TDP-43 loss significantly upregulated insertion of PKN1-5a1 in M17, HEK-293T, HeLa, and iNeurons, whereas the A3SS event was detectable only in M17 cells (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Fig. 1c, d) and was expressed at a much lower level than 5a1. This suggests that TDP-43’s suppression of aberrant splicing of PKN1-5a1 is more conserved.

To directly visualize the expression of PKN1-5a1 splicing product at the cellular level, we introduced a dCas13a-GFP (green fluorescent protein) system for detection32,33. This system is based on a Cas13a variant from Leptotrichia wadei (dead LwaCas13a, dCas13a) whose nuclease activity is inactivated but which can still recognize target RNA under the guidance of a specific crRNA and form a fluorescent signal with GFP, thereby enabling spatial localization of target RNA molecules (Fig. 1f). We designed two crRNAs (designated crRNA-1 and crRNA-2) that recognize different regions of PKN1-5a1, with crRNA-1 targeting the junction between 5a1 and exon 4 and crRNA-2 targeting the junction between 5a1 and exon 5 (Fig. 1g). To ensure accessibility for binding, we used MFold34 to predict the secondary structure of the RNA sequence of the PKN1-5a1 splicing product. The results showed that the sequences targeted by crRNA-1 and crRNA-2 were both located in single-stranded loop/bulge regions exposed on the RNA surface, displaying good accessibility suitable for dCas13a binding (Fig. 1g). We then co-transfected the dCas13a-GFP system with either crRNA-1 or crRNA-2 into TDP-43–knockdown HEK-293T cells. After cell fixation, TDP-43 was detected by immunostaining using a TDP-43 antibody to assess knockdown efficiency, and the dCas13a-GFP signal was visualized with a GFP antibody. We found that magenta fluorescence was markedly reduced in the TDP-43–knockdown group, indicating a clear decrease in its expression. Meanwhile, distinct green fluorescent puncta were observed predominantly in the nuclei of TDP-43–deficient cells, whereas no obvious signal was detected in the control group (Fig. 1h and Supplementary Fig. 1e). Quantification of green puncta per cell further showed a significant increase in the number of dCas13a-GFP puncta in the shTDP-43 group (Fig. 1i and Supplementary Fig. 1f), suggesting that this cryptic splicing product is activated under TDP-43 deficiency and can be specifically recognized and visualized.

More importantly, we found that TDP-43 knockdown significantly reduced PKN1 protein level (Fig. 1j and Supplementary Fig. 1g-i). We therefore constructed a dual-fluorescence, splicing-dependent translation reporter system to verify the impact of PKN1-5a1 insertion on translation. In this system, EGFP expression serves as an internal control, whereas mCherry expression depends on whether splicing proceeds normally. Once the PKN1-5a1 exon is inserted, the introduction of premature termination codons blocks downstream mCherry translation (Fig. 1k). After co-transfection of this system with shTDP-43 or shCTR into HEK-293T cells, Western blots showed that mCherry protein was completely absent in the TDP-43 knockdown group (Supplementary Fig. 1k); flow cytometry further showed that before knockdown, double-positive (mCherry and EGFP) cells accounted for 57.75%, whereas after knockdown, this proportion was decreased to 11.37% (Fig. 1l). These results suggest that insertion of PKN1-5a1 interrupts downstream translation, thereby aborting PKN1 protein synthesis.

To further verify whether deletion of cryptic exon 5a1 could rescue the decline in PKN1 protein levels under TDP-43 deficiency, we constructed two reporter plasmids: PK-intron (containing exons 4 and 5, and the full intronic interval between them, including 5a1) and PK-Δ5a1 (in the same background but with the 5a1 region specifically removed) (Fig. 1m). After co-transfecting these two plasmids with shTDP-43 into HEK-293T cells and performing Western blots analysis, we found that under TDP-43 knockdown, PKN1 protein expression was markedly reduced only in the PK-intron group, whereas remained essentially unchanged in the PK-Δ5a1 group (Fig. 1n). Interestingly, a 25–33 kDa FLAG band was appeared under TDP-43 knockdown in the PK-intron group, but no such band in the PK-Δ5a1 group (Fig. 1n). Together, these results indicate that insertion of PKN1-5a1 is the direct cause of the downregulation of PKN1 expression in the context of TDP-43 loss.

TDP-43 knockdown reduces PKN1 protein expression in mice but does not activate the PKN1-5a1 cryptic splicing

Given that the PKN1-5a1 splicing event is markedly activated under TDP-43 deficiency, we further investigated the evolutionary conservation of this exon and its expression characteristics in mouse models. The results showed that PKN1-5a1 is highly conserved in primates but lacks a corresponding conserved sequence in mice (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b). This feature is similar to previously reported cryptic splicing events in STMN2 and UNC13A13,15, which likewise are conserved in humans or primates but absent or not spliced in mice, suggesting that such TDP-43–dependent cryptic splicing regulation exhibits pronounced species specificity during evolution.

Nevertheless, by immunofluorescence staining and Western blots, we observed a significant decrease in PKN1 protein levels in the hippocampus of TDP-43–knockdown mice (Supplementary Fig. 2c, d). However, IGV analysis and RT-PCR in TDP-43–knockdown N2a cells did not reveal obvious changes in PKN1 splicing patterns or mRNA levels (Supplementary Fig. 2e). We speculate that TDP-43 knockdown may affect PKN1 protein stability in mouse cells. To test this hypothesis, after knocking down TDP-43 in N2a cells, we used cycloheximide (CHX) to inhibit protein translation and collected samples at 0, 4, 8, and 12 hours, assessing PKN1 expression by Western blots. We found that PKN1 protein was already decreased at 0 hours in shTDP-43 N2a cells, and its degradation rate accelerated significantly over time (Supplementary Fig. 2f). Although the rat genome harbors splice sites in this region that conform to the GU–AG rule, the overall sequence is not conserved relative to the human PKN1-5a1 region. Using non–exon-spanning primers for RT-PCR in TDP-43–knockdown rat B104 cells, we likewise did not observe bands other than the constitutively spliced product (Supplementary Fig. 2g). These results suggest that the presence of GU–AG splice signals alone is insufficient to drive cryptic exon splicing; the occurrence of the event may depend on higher-order cis-regulatory information.

In summary, although PKN1-5a1 lacks splicing activity in rodents, TDP-43 knockdown still induces a reduction of PKN1 protein expression in mouse brain tissue; this regulatory mechanism may involve protein stability rather than changes at the transcriptional or splicing level. These results suggest that TDP-43 regulation of PKN1 is markedly species-specific, and the physiological and pathological significance of its cryptic splicing remains to be further validated in primate models.

PKN1 cryptic exon in ALS neurons

In recent years, cryptic splicing events have been increasingly recognized as potentially disease-specific and important molecular markers in neurodegenerative disorders17–19,21,22,29. Accordingly, we analyzed the publicly available ALS brain RNA-seq dataset (GSE153960) from the New York Genome Center (NYGC), and investigated the activation of PKN1 cryptic exon 5a1 to assess its clinical relevance as a candidate biomarker of ALS.

First, using RNA-seq reads covering all known PKN1 exons, we estimated full-length transcript expression with TPM (transcripts per million). Given that PKN1 has multiple splicing isoforms and sequencing depth varies across samples, TPM—being length-normalized—reflects within-sample abundance and is suitable for cross-sample comparisons, making it preferable for full-length transcript–level analyses. PKN1 expression was reduced not only in regions classically affected by TDP-43 pathology4,35,36, e.g., frontal cortex, temporal cortex, motor cortex, and cervical/lumbar spinal cord; but, interestingly, also showed a similar trend in the cerebellum, which is typically considered less impacted by TDP-43 (Fig. 2a). This suggests that downregulation may not be solely attributable to loss of TDP-43 function. Given that PKN1 is a phosphor-protein involved in neuronal cytoskeletal regulation24,25, we speculated that reduced PKN1 expression in the cerebellum may reflect broader neurodegenerative processes such as neuronal loss. We also noted varying degrees of PKN1 reduction in some “Other” group samples, although statistical differences were comparatively modest.

To delineate the regional distribution of PKN1 splicing abnormalities, we quantified PKN1-5a1 expression. Specifically, for the hg38 interval chr19:14,450,088–14,450,214, we calculated RPM (reads per million) as a relative measure of the cryptic exon. Compared with length-dependent metrics (e.g., TPM/FPKM), RPM is more appropriate for fixed loci such as cryptic exons, effectively controlling for between-sample depth differences and widely used for exon- or event-level quantification. Preliminary analyses detected reads over this interval in a subset of healthy controls (a read was counted toward PKN1-5a1 if ≥75% of its aligned length overlapped the 127-bp 5a1 region). However, junction-level visualization revealed that these signals largely arose from a low-abundance A3SS event (chr19:14,450,088–14,450,317) that shares the same 5′ donor with 5a1 (Fig. 1a), causing some junction reads to be misassigned to PKN1-5a1 and generating false positives in RPM analysis. To avoid A3SS contamination, we computed an endpoint-strict CE-pair RPM from RegTools/LeafCutter counts—counting only Exon4→CE and CE→Exon5 and discarding A3SS-exclusive junctions—which strengthened specificity and the reliability of between-region comparisons (see ‘Methods’).

After correction, PKN1-5a1 was significantly upregulated across multiple CNS regions in ALS, with the most pronounced changes in canonical disease sites—frontal cortex, temporal cortex, motor cortex, and cervical and lumbar spinal cord—whereas no clear changes were observed in the cerebellum (Fig. 2b). By contrast, the cryptic exon was virtually absent in healthy controls, supporting strong disease specificity. In the “Other” group, a subset of individuals also showed elevated PKN1-5a1, particularly in cortical regions, with levels intermediate between ALS and normal control (NC). This may indicate TDP-43 dysfunction in certain atypical cases, but this hypothesis requires further histological or molecular-pathological validation. Overall, PKN1-5a1 expression is concentrated in cortex and spinal cord—regions heavily affected by TDP-43 pathology4,35,36—and remains low in the typically less affected cerebellum. This spatial pattern aligns with the regional selectivity of TDP-43 pathology in ALS, and further supports PKN1-5a1 as a candidate biomarker of TDP-43 proteinopathies–associated splicing abnormalities.

TDP-43 suppresses cryptic splicing of PKN1 through direct binding to conserved UG-rich elements in intron 5

As an aberrant splicing event abundantly detected in ALS patients (Fig. 2b), PKN1-5a1 has potential value as a target for intervention. Therefore, we further focused on the regulatory role of TDP-43 in the splice selection of PKN1, exploring how it finely regulates the generation of this cryptic exon through binding to pre-mRNA, with the aim of providing a theoretical basis for mechanistic understanding and the development of subsequent therapeutic strategies.

To test this hypothesis, we analyzed TDP-43 CLIP-seq data in the POSTAR3 database37. The results showed multiple high-confidence TDP-43 binding sites in the intronic region between exons 4 and 5 of PKN1, these sites are enriched for UG-repeat sequences and were ranked from high to low according to the crosslinking-induced truncation site (CITS) score (Fig. 3a). We further performed RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) in M17 cells. Compared with the IgG control, TDP-43 specifically enriched PKN1 transcripts containing the 5a1 region (Fig. 3b), supporting the existence of direct binding between TDP-43 and PKN1 pre-mRNA in cells.

To clarify the functional significance of these TDP-43 binding sites in regulating PKN1 cryptic splicing, we constructed a minigene containing exon 4, intron 5, and exon 5 of PKN1 (PKmini), and co-transfected with shTDP-43 or shCTR into HEK-293T cells. RT-PCR analysis showed that under shTDP-43 condition, in addition to the normal splicing product, the cryptic splicing product PKN1-5a1 was detected, whereas only normal splice form was produced in the shCTR group (Fig. 3c). This result not only validated the repressive role of TDP-43 in this cryptic splicing event, but also indicated that the PKmini system can be served as an important tool for analyzing downstream splicing regulatory mechanisms.

To further characterize TDP-43 regulatory sites, we predicted six conserved binding sites based on the CLIP-seq results (site1–site6), among which sites 1–5 are located upstream of the cryptic exon PKN1-5a1 and site 6 downstream (Fig. 3a). Based on this structural feature, we prioritized constructing mutant minigenes lacking site1–5 (PKmini^D1–5) (Fig. 3d) or lacking site 6 (PKmini^D6) (Fig. 3h). RT-PCR results showed that PKmini^D1–5 markedly induced the cryptic splicing product PKN1-5a1 (Fig. 3e), whereas PKmini^D6 primarily produced an A3SS product (Fig. 3i). Sanger sequencing further validated the splice junctions of these aberrant events (Supplementary Fig. 3a), indicating that deletion of distinct TDP-43 binding sites can regulate PKN1 splice selection through specific mechanisms. To further verify the functional role of TDP-43 in the above splicing regulation, we performed TDP-43 overexpression and knockdown on the background of PKmini^D1–5 or PKmini^D6, respectively. The results showed that TDP-43 overexpesssion significantly suppressed aberrant splicing in both mutants and enhanced normal splicing (Fig. 3g, k); conversely, TDP-43 knockdown further increased aberrant splicing (Fig. 3f, j). Notably, when querying human SNP databases (e.g., dbSNP), we found that although these variants are not associated with specific diseases, multiple SNPs annotated as nonpathogenic are located in the site 6 region (Supplementary Fig. 3b). To further assess their functional impact, we constructed mutant minigenes containing the above SNPs, and these variants likewise induced aberrant splicing events in the minigene (Supplementary Fig. 3c), further supporting site 6 as one of the key cis-acting elements regulating PKN1 splicing.

To clarify the cis-acting mechanism of the site 1–6 regions in TDP-43–dependent splicing regulation, we constructed a mutant simultaneously lacking all six sites (PKmini^D1–6) (Fig. 3l). In this construct, the A3SS event could still occur, but the responsiveness to TDP-43 expression level was completely lost (Fig. 3m), i.e., neither overexpression nor knockdown of TDP-43 significantly altered its splicing pattern. By contrast, on the PKmini^D6 background lacking only site 6, TDP-43 expression still effectively regulated A3SS splicing levels (Fig. 3j, k). Given that TDP-43 could still regulate A3SS splicing when only site 6 was deleted, whereas this regulation was completely lost when sites 1–6 were deleted, these results suggest that TDP-43 regulation of A3SS splicing may depend on cis-acting elements in the site 1–5 region, whereas site 6 is more likely involved in selection of the A3SS acceptor site, thereby influencing the final splicing outcome. To further pinpoint key cis elements, we generated multiple combinatorial deletion mutants (e.g., PKmini^D1+6, PKmini^D2+6, etc.) (Fig. 3l) and systematically evaluated their effects on the A3SS event. PSI analysis showed that among all the combinations, deletion of site 3 or site 5 led to a more pronounced reduction in TDP-43’s ability to suppress aberrant splicing (Fig. 3m), suggesting that these two sites may be key cis elements mediating TDP-43 splicing regulation.

Finally, to determine whether TDP-43 directly binds specific sites on the pre-mRNA of PKN1, we designed biotin-labeled RNA probes covering the site 1–site 6 regions (Fig. 3n) and performed electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA). We incubated the probes with recombinant TDP-43 protein. In native polyacrylamide gels, we observed distinct nucleic acid–protein complex bands for TDP-43 with site 1, site 2, site 3, site 5, and site 6, indicating binding capability at these sites (Fig. 3o), whereas site 4 showed no complex formation, suggesting no obvious affinity for this region. In addition, to further verify the binding specificity and affinity between TDP-43 and the candidate cis elements, we performed EMSA assay for each probe under different TDP-43 concentrations. We found that as TDP-43 concentration was increased, the intensity of complex bands formed with the probes of site 1, site 2, site 3, site 5, and site 6 were increased significantly in a typical dose-dependent manner (Supplementary Fig. 3d), indicating stable and specific binding. Conversely, site 4 showed no complex band even at high TDP-43 concentrations, further indicating a lack of binding to TDP-43. Together, these results indicate that TDP-43 precisely regulates PKN1 splicing by directly binding multiple conserved sites on the pre-mRNA of PKN1, thereby suppressing production of cryptic exon 5a1 and maintaining the correct splicing of PKN1 mRNA (Fig. 3p).

The RRM1 domain and dimerization capacity jointly maintain the fidelity of TDP-43 regulation on PKN1 splicing

To delineate the structural basis by which TDP-43 regulates PKN1 cryptic splicing, we systematically evaluated the functional roles of its dimerization capacity and RNA-recognition domains in this process. Although previous studies have indicated that the dimeric state of TDP-43 influences its RNA splicing function, the mechanistic underpinnings in specific cryptic splicing events remain to be clarified29,38. To test whether this structural basis controls PKN1 splicing, we overexpressed dimerization-impaired mutant, TDP-43^90–414 (90-414), and TDP-43^N6A (N6A), a dimerization-defective N-terminal mutant carrying six alanine substitutions38–40 in HEK-293T cells. Cells were then treated with the cell-permeable dimer crosslinker disuccinimidyl glutarate (DSG) and analyzed by Western blots. We found that full-length TDP-43 (TDP-43^FL) formed stable dimers and higher-ordered oligomers, whereas 90–414 and N6A existed predominantly as monomers, with virtually no crosslinked bands (Fig. 4a), confirming markedly impaired dimerization for both mutants. Functionally, when 90–414 or N6A was co-transfected with the splicing reporter PKmini into HEK-293T cells without endogenous TDP-43 knockdown, neither mutant induced insertion of PKN1-5a1 (Fig. 4b). However, upon TDP-43 knockdown, both mutants failed to effectively suppress insertion of the cryptic exon PKN1-5a1 (Fig. 4c), whereas TDP-43^FL significantly suppressed this cryptic splicing event under the same conditions, indicating that loss of dimerization weakens the splicing regulatory function of TDP-43.

TDP-43 contains two conserved RNA recognition motifs (RRMs), among which RRM1 is considered central to RNA binding and splicing regulation41. To validate the role of RRMs in PKN1 splicing, we co-transfected TDP-43^FL, loss-of-function mutant of RRM1 (F147/149L) or RRM2 (F227/229L), deletion mutant of RRM1 (ΔRRM1) or RRM2 (ΔRRM2) with PKmini into HEK-293T cells, and analyzed by RT-PCR. Interestingly, we found that F147/149L and ΔRRM1 both markedly induced aberrant insertion of PKN1-5a1, with the effects resembling TDP-43 knockdown, particularly pronounced for ΔRRM1 (Fig. 4b), suggesting a dominant-negative effect of RRM1 deletion. Similarly, upon a TDP-43 knockdown background (Supplementary Fig. 4a), co-transfection of these mutants with PKmini into HEK-293T cells revealed that TF147/149L and ΔRRM1 failed to suppress PKN1-5a1 insertion, consistent with the loss-of-function phenotype (Fig. 4c). Moreover, ΔRRM1 not only failed to suppress the cryptic event but further enhanced PKN1-5a1 insertion. Notably, even without PKmini transfection, overexpression of ΔRRM1 in HEK-293T cells significantly induced insertion of 5a1 in the endogenous PKN1 transcript (Fig. 4d), further indicating that the ΔRRM1 mutant interferes with normal regulation of endogenous splice sites through a dominant-negative mechanism. In addition, we observed that F147/149L and ΔRRM1 formed aberrant nuclear condensates and colocalized with TDP-43^FL in HEK-293T cells, as previously describe42–44, whereas other constructs (e.g., TDP-43^FL, F227/229L, or ΔRRM2) did not form nuclear condensates (Supplementary Fig. 4b).

Previous studies have shown that dominant-negative mutants can heterodimerize with the wild-type counterparts, thereby impairing normal function45. Together with the prior finding that the N terminus of TDP-43 has dimerization capacity38–40, we further hypothesized that ΔRRM1 might exert dominant-negative effects by forming heterodimers with endogenous wild-type TDP-43, thereby disrupting recognition and binding of RNA targets. To test this hypothesis, we generated a double mutant lacking both dimerization capacity and RRM1 (ΔRRM1^N6A), and co-transfected with PKmini into HEK-293T cells, then analyzed by RT-PCR. We found that, unlike ΔRRM1—which markedly induced PKN1-5a1 insertion—ΔRRM1^N6A did not elicit obvious cryptic exon insertion, indicating a lack of dominant-negative activity (Fig. 4e). To further determine whether these mutants retain the ability to associate with wild-type TDP-43, we employed the bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) system. TDP-43 and each mutant were fused to Venus N-terminal fragment 173 (VN173) or Venus C-terminal fragment 155 (VC155) fragments of the BiFC system, and co-expressed in HEK-293T cells. If dimerization occurs, the VN and VC fragments will produce a GFP signal. We found that TDP-43-VN173 and TDP-43-VC155 generated strong nuclear GFP signals, confirming homodimerization; ΔRRM1-VC155 also formed heterodimers with TDP-43-VN173; by contrast, N6A-VC155 and ΔRRM1^N6A-VC155 failed to induce GFP signals, indicating complete loss of dimerization capacity and further indicating that RRM1 forms heterodimers with wild-type TDP-43 via the N terminus (Supplementary Fig. 4c).

We had previously observed that ΔRRM1 formed pronounced nuclear condensates and colocalized with wild-type TDP-43 (WT), and, together with the ability of ΔRRM1 to form heterodimers with WT, we hypothesized that ΔRRM1 might recruit WT into the aberrant nuclear condensates formed via dimerization. To test this, we designed two key conditions: (1) whether ΔRRM1 condensates recruit TDP-43-VN173/ΔRRM1-VC155 heterodimers efficiently; and (2) whether these condensates recruit TDP-43-VN173/TDP-43-VC155 homodimers. We co-transfected TDP-43-VN173 with ΔRRM1-VC155 or TDP-43-VC155, and ΔRRM1 mutant into HEK-293T cells. Fluorescence imaging of living cells showed robust BiFC punctate signals in the TDP-43-VN173/ΔRRM1-VC155 and ΔRRM1 group, whereas only weak BiFC punctate signals were observed in the TDP-43-VN173/TDP-43-VC155 and ΔRRM1 group (Fig. 4f). Given that the fluorescences in BiFC system are arised from stabilized protein–protein interactions, these results suggest that ΔRRM1 condensates preferentially recruit TDP-43/ΔRRM1 heterodimers rather than TDP-43 homodimers (Fig. 4g). To determine whether ΔRRM1 is specific for this BiFC punctate signals, we performed parallel control experiments by co-expressing wild-type TDP-43 and TDP-43-VN173 with either ΔRRM1-VC155 or TDP-43-VC155; no similar nuclear puncta were observed (Supplementary Fig. 4d), further supporting ΔRRM1 as the key driver of the aberrant aggregation of TDP-43. Whether such condensates functionally “sequester” wild-type TDP-43 and thereby impair its binding to PKN1 pre-mRNA remain to be further validated using the MS2–MCP system46.

Taken together, these results support our hypothesis that TDP-43^ΔRRM1 can form heterodimers with endogenous TDP-43 via its retained N-terminal region, thereby disrupting normal recognition and binding to RNA targets and inducing aberrant splicing through a dominant-negative mechanism, whereas N-terminal dimerization–deficient mutations effectively block this process (Fig. 4h).

TDP-43 knockdown generates and accumulates the cryptic peptide PKN1-N207

Previously, we knocked down TDP-43 in HEK-293T cells expressing PK-intron, and observed a ~25–33 kDa FLAG band (Fig. 1n), suggesting that an aberrant transcript arising from a cryptic splicing event might be translated into a truncated cryptic peptide. Interestingly, this splicing product contains a PTC (Supplementary Fig. 1a) and should be subject to NMD47. However, the stable presence of this band implies that it may partially escape NMD.

To test this hypothesis, we treated TDP-43–knockdown HEK-293T cells with the translation inhibitor CHX (2 μg/mL) to indirectly inhibit NMD activity and performed to qRT-PCR analysis. We found that PKN1-5a1 expression was increased ~1.4-fold in the CHX group, compared with the DMSO group (Supplementary Fig. 5a). Furthermore, we knocked down up-frameshift protein 1 (UPF1), a key effector of NMD48 (Fig. 5a), to specifically block this pathway. We found that UPF1 knockdown alone did not induce aberrant splicing of PKN1-5a1, but in the context of TDP-43 deficiency, combined UPF1 knockdown further upregulated its expression by ~1.6-fold (Fig. 5a), supporting that PKN1-5a1 transcript can be partially recognized and degraded by NMD. Notably, either by CHX treatment or UPF1 knockdown, the magnitude of PKN1-5a1 upregulation was limited; together with our previous observation of the “FLAG band”. These suggest that PKN1-5a1 may not be a typical NMD target and may escape degradation by being translated into a truncated peptide. This, of course, required validation at the endogenous level. Therefore, we generated stable TDP-43–knockdown HEK-293T and M17 cell lines. Specifically, cells were infected with lenti/shTDP-43, treated with puromycin (2 μg/mL) for 4 days, and then cultured without antibiotics for an additional 6 days. It should be noted that TDP-43 knockdown markedly suppressed the proliferative capacity of HEK-293T and M17 cells, making long-term stable passaging difficult. To assess proliferation, we performed an EdU incorporation assay on HEK-293T cells at day 10 post-infection. We found a clear decrease in cell density and a significant reduction in EdU-positive cells in the shTDP-43 group (Supplementary Fig. 5b), indicating impaired proliferation, consistent with previous studies49. We then collected the selected HEK-293T and M17 cells for Western blots analysis, using a specific antibody against the N terminus of PKN1 to monitor the expression of full-length PKN1 and the truncated peptide. We found that TDP-43 knockdown led to a marked decrease in full-length PKN1, accompanied by a pronounced increase in a truncated peptide within the 25~33 kDa range (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 5c). Based on the splice junctions and reading frame, this band corresponds to the first 207 amino acids of PKN1; we therefore designated the cryptic peptide PKN207. To further analyze its accumulation at different time points, we set a time course of TDP-43 knockdown at 48, 72, 96, and 120 hours, and performed to Western blots. We found that full-length PKN1 was gradually decreased from 48 hours onward, but the PKN207 band was clearly detected only after 120 hours of sustained TDP-43 deficiency (Fig. 5c), suggesting that this truncated peptide must gradually accumulate under continuous loss of TDP-43 to reach a detectable level.

To further evaluate the stability of this cryptic peptide PKN207 in HEK-293T cells, we constructed a Tet-on inducible expression system to drive expression of full-length PKN1 (Tet-PKFL) and the N207 cryptic peptide (Tet-PKN207), respectively (Fig. 5d). After induction with doxycycline (Dox, 1 μg/mL) for 24 hours, the medium was replaced with Dox-free medium, then treated with CHX (2 μg/mL); cells were collected at 0, 4, 8, and 12 hours for immunoblotting. We found that with prolonged CHX treatment, full-length PKN1 levels were gradually declined, while PKN207 levels remained stable throughout (Fig. 5d), indicating that PKN207 cryptic peptide has high intracellular stability and may continuously accumulate in HEK-293T cells (Fig. 4g). Furthermore, we simultaneously knocked down TDP-43 and PKN1 in HEK-293T cells to examine changes in PKN207 expression. We observed that TDP-43 knockdown markedly enhanced PKN207 expression, whereas concurrent PKN1 knockdown clearly reduced the truncated peptide (Fig. 5e), further demonstrating that it originates from aberrant splicing of the PKN1 gene. These results indicate that the TDP-43–knockdown–induced cryptic splicing of PKN1 can, after prolonged accumulation, generate and express the cryptic peptide PKN207, and that this peptide exhibits high stability, suggesting that it may persistently exert functions in cells.

A specific antibody reveals that the PKN207 cryptic peptide is detectable in AD brain with TDP-43 pathology

Given that the PKN1-5a1 cryptic exon has been validated in RNA-seq data of ALS cohort from NYGC, we further hypothesized that whether this cryptic splicing event truly occurs in patients, its translation product—the PKN207 cryptic peptide—might also be detectable in patients with TDP-43 pathology. To test this hypothesis, we attempted to generate antibodies capable of specifically recognizing PKN207. Sequence alignment showed that the C terminus of PKN207 protein contains a unique amino acid sequence “LAL”, which replaces the “SPD” sequence present in full-length PKN1, resulting in a distinct C-terminal structure (Supplementary Fig. 5d). To maximize antibody specificity, we selected an eight–amino acid peptide, “DDTQGLAL”, spanning this differential region, as the immunogen. Structural predictions indicated that this region is surface-exposed and exhibits favorable antigenicity, hydrophilicity, and immunogenicity (Supplementary Fig. 5e). On this basis, we immunized rabbits intraperitoneally with the peptide and prepared four polyclonal anti-PKN207 antibodies (E29426–E29429) (Supplementary Fig. 5f).

To validate the specificity of the antibodies for PKN207, we overexpressed either full-length PKN1 (PKFL) or the PKN207 cryptic peptide in HEK-293T cells and performed to Western blots analysis. All four antibodies showed a specific band of approximately 27–33 kDa in the PKN207 group, while no signal in the PKFL group, indicating that these antibodies do not cross-react with full-length PKN1 (Fig. 5f). We then further validated their recognition in TDP-43–knockdown or control HEK-293T cells. All four antibodies showed a band of approximately 27 kDa in the shTDP-43 group, no obvious signal in the control group (Fig. 5g); among them, E29426 exhibited the lowest background and best specificity (Fig. 5g). These results indicate that this antibody series specifically recognize PKN207 but not PKFL. To further assess the cellular localization of PKN207, we overexpressed PKN1^FL or PKN1^N207 in HEK-293T cells, and performed to nuclear–cytoplasmic fractionation and Western blots. We found that PKN1 localized mainly in the cytoplasm with a portion in the nucleus, whereas PKN207 localized exclusively in the cytoplasm (Supplementary Fig. 5g). We next evaluated the applicability of these antibodies in immunofluorescence staining. We transfected PKN207-EGFP into HEK-293T cells and performed immunostaining with the four antibodies (red fluorescence). We observed strong diffuse cytoplasmic red signals regardless of EGFP transfection (Supplementary Fig. 5h–k), indicating notable nonspecific background of these polyclonal antibodies in immunofluorescence.

We ultimately selected the E29426 antibody to determine whether it could be used to detect PKN207 expression in patients with TDP-43 pathology. Given that ALS brain tissue was unavailable and TDP-43 pathology is present in ~20–50% of AD patients7,50,51, we examined hippocampal tissue from TDP-43-positive AD cases. First, we assessed the presence of phosphorylated TDP-43 (pTDP-43) in the RIPA-insoluble fraction of AD samples by Western blots. We found clear pTDP-43 signals in AD1 and AD5, indicating typical TDP-43 proteinopathy (Fig. 5h). We then examined PKN207 expression in the AD samples. Although there was no significant difference in PKFL between the AD and control groups (Fig. 5i), we detected a distinct ~25–33 kDa band in AD1 and AD5 using the E29426 antibody, whereas no such band was observed in the control group or in TDP-43-negative AD cases (Fig. 5h, j). Further RT-PCR analysis also showed that the PKN1-5a1 cryptic exon was detected in AD1, AD2, and AD5 (Fig. 5k). Notably, PKN207 expression mirrored pTDP-43 pathology, being present in AD1 and AD5 (which showed marked aggregation) but absent in AD2 and controls (which lacked corresponding pathology) (Fig. 5j). In contrast, the PKN1-5a1 cryptic exon transcript was detected at low levels in AD2 as well (Fig. 5k), yet no corresponding PKN207 protein was detected, demonstrating that cryptic splicing does not always produce a stable protein. We speculate that even in the absence of classic aggregated pTDP-43, functional abnormalities of TDP-43 (e.g., mild nuclear loss or weakened splicing regulatory capacity) may still occur in AD2, thereby inducing activation of specific cryptic splicing. This splicing abnormality may represent an early molecular feature of TDP-43 loss of function that has not yet progressed to visible aggregate pathology. In addition, the splicing product may not yet have accumulated to a detectable protein level in vivo, leading to failure to detect the corresponding PKN207 band. In summary, compared with the splicing event itself, the expression of PKN207 cryptic peptide may more directly reflect TDP-43 pathology, and the E29426 antibody holds promise as a more specific biomarker for TDP-43 proteinopathies.

Expression of the PKN207 cryptic peptide induces cognitive impairment in mice

We detected the expression of PKN207 cryptic peptide in TDP-43-positive AD brains, whereas PKFL showed no obvious change (Fig. 5h), suggesting that PKN207 may directly mediate neuronal dysfunction without altering full-length protein expression, and may even participate in the development of cognitive impairment. Given the limited number of AD samples in the immunoblot analysis, we further analyzed RNA-seq data from the parahippocampal gyrus (PHG) in the Mount Sinai Brain Bank (MSBB) AD transcriptome database to expand the sample size and validate the finding at the transcriptional level. We found that the PKN1-5a1 cryptic exon was stably detected in AD patients, and nearly absent in healthy controls (Fig. 6a), supporting its activation in disease and potential pathogenicity. Meanwhile, full-length PKN1 mRNA expression was slightly increased, which may explain the lack of a significant change at the protein level. Notably, activation of this cryptic splicing event was observed even at Braak stage 1, an early stage of AD, suggesting that it may be induced at the early stage of the disease process.

To test the potential neurotoxicity of PKN207, we injected three neuron-specific promoter adeno-associated viruses (AAV-hSyn) into the hippocampus bilaterally of 2-month-old C57BL/6J mice: AAV-PKFL (encoding full-length PKN1), AAV-PKN207 (encoding the N207 cryptic peptide), and an empty control virus AAV-CTR (Fig. 6b). We also validated the expression of AAV-PKFL and AAV-PKN207 in the mouse hippocampus by Western blots, and confirmed robust expression of both PKFL and the PKN207 peptide (Supplementary Fig. 6e). Four months later, Morris water maze (MWM) testing showed significant cognitive deficits in both the AAV-PKFL and AAV-PKN207 groups (Fig. 6c), indicating that overexpression of either protein may adversely affect learning and memory.

Considering that cognitive impairment is often accompanied by structural damage to neuronal axons, we further measured NEFL level in CSF 4 months post virus injection. CSF-NEFL was significantly higher in the PKFL and N207 groups than in their respective control groups (Fig. 6d), suggesting compromised axonal integrity accompanied by increased neurofilament release. This change in a fluid biomarker reflects structural pathological alterations at the central nervous system level52–55.

To further verify whether PKN207 is cytotoxic, we overexpressed PKFL or PKN207 in primary mouse hippocampal neurons and assessed toxicity by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release. Cytotoxicity was significantly induced in both groups, with PKFL showing slightly higher toxicity than PKN207 (Fig. 6e). Nevertheless, as a splicing product specific to TDP-43 loss, PKN207 has a unique pathological context, suggesting that it may possess disease-state–specific pathogenic mechanisms.
